overview: The atlas’s Annam record covers 1000 to 1100, followed by Đại Việt from 1100 to 1815. These labels join a history of successive Vietnamese courts, beginning here with Early Lê and Lý rule; they do not name one unchanged dynasty. The medieval outline broadly covers northern and central Vietnam, but its southern edge is not a verified frontier for every year. Later outlines also conceal rival governments, especially after 1530. Colonial-era Annam is a separate record. Events and objects below retain their own dates.

periods.title: Early Lê rule
periods.summary: The first imported years fall in the final phase of Early Lê government, before Lý Công Uẩn took power.

periods.title: Lý rule
periods.summary: Lý rulers established their capital at Thăng Long in 1010; the dynasty continued across the map’s 1100 label change.

periods.title: Trần rule
periods.summary: The Trần court governed from Thăng Long for much of this period.

periods.title: Hồ rule and Ming occupation
periods.summary: The Hồ dynasty was followed by Ming occupation from 1407; withdrawal ended early in 1428.

periods.title: Early Lê dynasty
periods.summary: Lê rule followed the successful struggle against Ming occupation.

periods.title: Rival courts and changing rulers
periods.summary: Mạc and restored Lê regimes, Trịnh and Nguyễn lords, and Tây Sơn rulers complicate the map’s single label.

periods.title: Early Nguyễn transition
periods.summary: Gia Long reunited the country in 1802; Việt Nam became its name in 1804.

items.text: At the start of this map window, the Early Lê court ruled from Hoa Lư. Lý Công Uẩn’s accession in 1009 began a new dynasty. Royal succession could transform the court without creating a new population. The name Đại Cồ Việt continued until the adoption of Đại Việt in 1054.

In 1010, Lý Thái Tổ moved his capital from Hoa Lư to Đại La, renamed Thăng Long. The heritage authority reconstructs a river journey through connected waterways toward the Red River. Moving a government involved boats as well as buildings: the exhibition follows a travel route, not just an arrow between two dots.

Vietnamese rulers exchanged tribute, envoys and titles with the Song court while maintaining their own government. These relationships could alternate with armed conflict. A title bestowed by a neighboring emperor expressed a diplomatic hierarchy; it should not be confused with Song officials routinely running the Lý kingdom’s towns.

The Temple of Literature was founded in 1070, a court examination followed in 1075, and the Imperial Academy was established in 1076. Learning could open a route into royal service. These institutions were major developments in elite education, not evidence that every child attended school or sat an examination.

A short line in the capital-relocation edict attributed to Lý Thái Tổ in 1010 reads 其地廣而坦平: “Its land is broad and level.” The Sino-Vietnamese reading is Kỳ địa quảng nhi thản bình. This Classical Chinese text explains a choice of site. Here it follows a modern institutional edition of a transmitted work, not a surviving document in the king’s own handwriting.

The name Đại Việt was adopted under Lý Thánh Tông in 1054, within the earlier Annam map interval. It survived several dynastic changes, although the Hồ rulers used Đại Ngu. A familiar country name could outlast a ruling family; it should not make the many changes of government disappear.

Thăng Long’s Lý citadel was built on reclaimed ground in the Red River Delta, above remains of an earlier Chinese fortress. Excavations at 18 Hoàng Diệu reveal successive layers of buildings and objects. Archaeologists have to separate those layers: a seventh-century foundation and an eleventh-century palace tell different chapters of the same place.

In 1288, Trần commanders helped defeat a Yuan invasion by attacking its food supply and using the tidal waterways. The invaders temporarily occupied Thăng Long, but their retreating fleet met obstacles and ambushes on the Bạch Đằng River. The historical account describes submerged stakes exposed as the tide fell. Geography and supplies mattered as much as fighting strength.

After Ming occupation, Lê Lợi’s forces negotiated the withdrawal of the opposing army at Đông Quan in late 1427. The agreement included provisions for food, horses and boats so troops could leave. The last contingent departed in early 1428, and the Lê dynasty followed. The resolution involved negotiation and transport as well as battlefield victory.

The Mạc replaced the Lê court in 1527, but later Lê and Nguyễn histories often treated the Mạc as illegitimate usurpers. Museum historian Nguyễn Ngọc Chất points out that even hostile accounts preserve evidence of their examinations and administration. A dynasty’s reputation depends partly on who wrote its history afterward.

Trịnh lords ruled the north in the Lê kings’ name, while Nguyễn lords governed the south. Warfare from 1627 to 1672 left a lasting division near the Gianh River. Tây Sơn forces overthrew Trịnh power in 1786; their leader Nguyễn Huệ, Emperor Quang Trung, defeated a Qing intervention in 1789. These upheavals were far more complicated than the map’s single colored outline.

Lý builders reused earlier wells at Thăng Long rather than starting every water supply from scratch. Archaeologists recognized Lý bricks above older well structures. That is a practical household lesson on a royal scale: if a useful well is already there, rebuilding the whole thing may be unnecessary. These finds come from the palace area, not a survey of every village.

Trần-period wells at the citadel used bricks arranged diagonally in a herringbone pattern. The interlocking arrangement held the lining together without mortar. Some much smaller wells are interpreted by the heritage authority as ritual features rather than drinking-water sources. Shape and construction help archaeologists ask what a feature was actually for.

Potters working at Thăng Long made glazed vessels as well as architectural materials. Among the workshop waste preserved by the National Museum are bowls and plates fused together during firing. A stuck stack could be a potter’s disappointment and an archaeologist’s lucky find: it locates the work of making things, not just their later use.

An eleventh- to fourteenth-century white-glazed bowl in the museum’s study measures 16.5 centimeters across and has raised plant decoration inside. Five small support marks remain in its bowl. Such traces preserve how objects were supported in the kiln. Even an attractive dish can carry the fingerprints of its manufacturing process, although these are firing marks rather than actual fingers.

A fifteenth- or sixteenth-century Vietnamese dish in Singapore’s Asian Civilisations Museum shows a duck flying among water reeds, painted in cobalt blue beneath the glaze. Vietnamese ceramics reached buyers in places now called Indonesia, the Philippines and Malaysia. A familiar bird could travel across the sea on a plate, carried through trading networks far beyond its maker’s workshop.

Palace excavations also revealed drainage in Lý-period layers, alongside wells and building foundations. Water had to be brought into a busy royal complex and carried away again. These are tangible traces of managing a built environment; the identified drains alone do not establish that houses throughout the kingdom had toilets.

Betel-chewing utensils offer another glimpse of social life. The museum exhibition includes lime containers, trays and spittoons, and identifies surviving equipment from the Lý period onward. Later traditions connect betel with hospitality and weddings, but the objects should not make every later ceremony an eleventh-century custom. A small container can be evidence of conversation as well as craftsmanship.

sections.title: Examinations and a voice carved in stone

items.text: At Hanoi’s Temple of Literature, 82 stone steles record royal examinations held from 1442 to 1779. They were erected between 1484 and 1780, so the date of an examination is not always the date its stone was carved. Their inscriptions preserve successful candidates, examiners and the officials who prepared the monuments. The Tiến sĩ qualification belonged to this historical examination system.

A small writing sample is “人才國家之元氣,” meaning “talented people are the vital force of the state.” This is Classical Chinese in the scholarly transcription of Đào Cử’s inscription for the 1463 examination, carved in 1484. The phrase explains why the ruler should cultivate talent. It is an official written language here, not a claim that ordinary conversation sounded like the inscription.

That same inscription remembers about 1,400 candidates and 44 selected scholars in the 1463 examination. Names were announced and displayed, and successful candidates received clothing and a banquet. Passing was a public achievement, not merely a private mark on a sheet of paper. The inscription also warns graduates to live up to their reputations and serve the people.

sections.title: Later port households and medical learning

items.text: Hội An’s historic townscape preserves a clever arrangement for merchant households: buildings faced the street for customers and opened toward the river behind for loading boats. Timber houses stood close together, alongside markets and family worship buildings. The surviving pattern reflects the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, though many structures were repaired or renewed in the nineteenth. The river was effectively a delivery entrance.

The eighteenth-century physician Lê Hữu Trác came from a scholarly family, but left military life and returned to care for his elderly mother and his brother’s orphaned children. He became known as Hải Thượng Lãn Ông, the “lazy old man” of Hải Thượng. The nickname described his rejection of the race for status, rather than a lack of effort in studying and treating patients.

Lê Hữu Trác taught students who copied his medical writings by hand. His collected work covered childbirth, children’s illnesses, eye problems, injuries and medical ethics, alongside other subjects. He also organized opportunities for practitioners to exchange experience. These manuscripts reveal a culture of medical learning and concern for families; listing a historical treatment does not establish that it worked.

ending.text: The Annam record’s 1100 endpoint falls within continuing Lý rule, not a conquest or disappearance. In the longer sequence, Gia Long reunited the country in 1802 and Việt Nam became the state name in 1804. The Đại Việt record’s 1815 endpoint is another map cutoff during Nguyễn rule. Dynasties, capitals and official names changed while communities, crafts, learning and family life continued.
